The taught proof route supplies the essential connections.

content.prompt:
In the diagram to the right, $PQRS$ is a rhombus. Let $M$ be the point of intersection of the diagonals $QS$ and $PR$.

Prove that $QM=MS$, $PM=MR$ and $\angle QMR$ is a right angle, as presented earlier.

spec.description: Unfilled rhombus with four matching single side ticks, single arrows on PQ and SR, double arrows on QR and PS, and red dashed diagonals meeting at M. Ordinary source blue strokes become black under house style.
spec.mathematics: PQ=QR=RS=SP; PQ is parallel to SR; QR is parallel to PS; M lies on PR and QS.
spec.answerVisibility: Only supplied geometry and marks are visible; no right-angle mark or diagonal-half equality marks are added.

answer.short:
$QM=MS$, $PM=MR$ and $\angle QMR=90^\circ$.

A rhombus is a parallelogram, so its diagonals bisect each other. Angle bisection and the angle sum of a triangle establish perpendicularity.
answer.worked:
A rhombus is a parallelogram. In triangles $PQM$ and $RSM$:
$$\begin{align*}\angle QPM&=\angle SRM &&\text{(alternate angles, }PQ\parallel SR\text{)}\\\angle PQM&=\angle RSM &&\text{(alternate angles, }PQ\parallel SR\text{)}\\PQ&=RS &&\text{(sides of a rhombus).}\end{align*}$$
Thus $\triangle PQM\equiv\triangle RSM$ (AAS). Hence $QM=MS$ and $PM=MR$ (matching sides of congruent triangles).

For perpendicularity, $PQ=PS$, $QR=SR$ and $PR$ is common. Therefore $\triangle PQR\equiv\triangle PSR$ (SSS), so $\angle QRP=\angle PRS$.

Let $\angle RQS=\alpha$ and $\angle QRP=\beta$. Since $QR=RS$, the base angles of isosceles triangle $QRS$ give $\angle QSR=\alpha$. Also $\angle QRS=2\beta$. Therefore
$$\begin{align*}2\alpha+2\beta&=180^\circ &&\text{(angle sum of }\triangle QRS\text{)}\\\alpha+\beta&=90^\circ.\end{align*}$$
In triangle $QMR$,
$$\begin{align*}\angle QMR&=180^\circ-(\alpha+\beta)\\\angle QMR&=180^\circ-90^\circ\\\angle QMR&=90^\circ.\end{align*}$$
Thus the diagonals bisect each other at right angles.
